# The Lives of Stars

Predict first. Why does the Sun shine? Is it burning, like an enormous fire?
Slowly shrinking and heating up? Something nuclear? Commit to one, then
estimate how long a fire the size of the Sun could last.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- place a star on the H-R diagram and name its main groups;
- explain how fusion powers a main-sequence star, and why massive stars die young;
- predict how a star ends from its initial mass.

## The H-R Diagram {#the-hr-diagram}

From the last chapter, every star can be given two numbers: its
**luminosity** (total power output, from distance and apparent brightness)
and its **surface temperature** (from color or spectral class). Plot one
against the other for thousands of stars and they do not scatter at random.
The chart is the **Hertzsprung-Russell diagram**.

By tradition, luminosity goes up the vertical axis and temperature increases
to the **left**, so hot blue stars are on the left and cool red ones on the
right. Three groups stand out:

- **The main sequence**: a diagonal band from hot and bright (upper left) to
  cool and dim (lower right). About 90 percent of stars, the Sun included,
  sit here.
- **Giants and supergiants** (upper right): cool, yet very luminous. A cool
  star can only be that bright if it is enormous. Betelgeuse is a red
  supergiant.
- **White dwarfs** (lower left): hot, yet dim. They must be tiny, about the
  size of Earth. Sirius B is one.

## Hydrogen Into Helium {#fusion}

A chemical fire the size of the Sun would burn out in a few thousand years,
and rocks on Earth are billions of years old. The Sun runs on something far
more powerful: nuclear **fusion**.

In the core, at about 15 million kelvin, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium.
Four hydrogen nuclei make one helium nucleus with about 0.7 percent less mass,
and the missing mass becomes energy (E = mc squared). The Sun converts about
600 million tons of hydrogen every second and has enough in its core to keep
going for about 10 billion years in all.

A main-sequence star is a balance. Gravity pulls every part of the star
inward; the pressure of the hot gas pushes outward. Squeeze a balloon between
your hands and you feel the same standoff. While the core has hydrogen, the
two stay balanced and the star stays steady.

A star's **mass** sets its place on the main sequence, and its lifetime.
Massive stars have more fuel but burn it enormously faster, like a truck with
a bigger tank and a much bigger engine:

| Initial mass | Main-sequence lifetime (rough) |
|---|---|
| 0.5 Suns | more than 50 billion years |
| 1 Sun | about 10 billion years |
| 10 Suns | a few tens of millions of years |

## How Stars Die {#stellar-endpoints}

When the core runs out of hydrogen, gravity gains ground. The core contracts
and heats, hydrogen keeps fusing in a shell around it, and the outer layers
swell and cool: the star becomes a **red giant**, moving up and to the right on
the H-R diagram. The Sun will do this in about 5 billion years.

What happens next depends on the star's initial mass:

- **Below about 8 solar masses** (the Sun included): the outer layers drift
  away as a glowing planetary nebula, and the core is left as a **white
  dwarf**.
- **Above about 8 solar masses**: the core collapses and the star explodes as
  a **supernova**, leaving a **neutron star**, about 20 km across.
- **The most massive stars**, roughly 20 solar masses and up: the collapsed
  core becomes a **black hole**.

The dividing masses are approximate, and astronomers still argue about the
exact values. The Sun is far too small to become a black hole.

::: {.callout-note title="Dr. Morgan's note"}
The iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones were made inside stars
and scattered by their deaths. Next time someone tells you that you are made
of stardust, you can tell them which kind.
:::

## Self-check

```{=html}
<div class="quiz" data-answer="b">
  <div class="question">1. A star has a surface of 3,500 K and 10,000 times the Sun's luminosity. Where is it on the H-R diagram?</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> Lower left, with the white dwarfs</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> Upper right, with the giants and supergiants</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> Upper left, at the top of the main sequence</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> Lower right, at the bottom of the main sequence</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>b</strong>. Cool (on the right) yet very luminous (high up), so it must be huge: a red giant or supergiant.
  </div>
</div>

<div class="quiz" data-answer="c">
  <div class="question">2. How will the Sun end?</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> As a black hole</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> In a supernova, leaving a neutron star</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> As a white dwarf, after a red giant stage</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> It will shine forever</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>c</strong>. The Sun is well below 8 solar masses, so it sheds its outer layers and leaves a white dwarf.
  </div>
</div>
```

## Where this fits

The stars in this chapter live in galaxies. Next we step back to look at our
own galaxy from the inside, and at the matter in it we cannot see.
